opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of compression as a really useful lens rather than the whole story.

The basic idea goes back to information theory. If you train a model to predict the next token, its log loss on a dataset is, quite literally, the number of bits you'd need to encode that data using the model as your compressor. So when we say a model gets better at pre-training, we're saying it's finding a shorter description of the data. And the claim that I find compelling is that to compress something really well, you need to understand the processes that generated it.

Think about what's in text on the internet. It's not random strings; it's the output of people reasoning, doing math, writing code, telling stories, arguing, describing the physical world. If you want to predict the next line of a proof, the cheapest way to do it eventually is to actually be able to do the math. If you want to predict what a character in a novel says next, you have to model their beliefs and intentions. So as you push the compression further, you're forced to internalize more and more of the structure behind the data, and a lot of that structure is what we'd call intelligence.

There's also a nice property about compression as an objective: it's very hard to game. With benchmarks, you can overfit, you can contaminate, you can teach to the test. But compression over a huge, held-out, diverse stream of data is a pretty honest signal. If your bits per token go down on genuinely new data, you've learned something real about the world. That's part of why it's been such a reliable north star for scaling: you see the loss go down smoothly, and downstream capabilities tend to emerge along with it.

Now, I'd add some nuance. Compression is necessary, but I don't think it's sufficient on its own to get you all the way to AGI in the practical sense. A few reasons. First, not all bits are equally valuable: a lot of the loss is spent on things like formatting, names, trivia, noise, while the bits that encode deep reasoning might be a small fraction. So the aggregate number can hide where the meaningful progress is. Second, a great compressor is a great predictor of the data distribution, but being useful means acting, pursuing goals, being reliable over long horizons, and knowing when you're wrong. That's where post-training, reinforcement learning, and inference-time reasoning come in. They take the rich world model you got from compression and shape it into something that can actually think through problems step by step and get things done.

So the way I'd put it: pre-training compression builds the foundation. It's how the model acquires its knowledge and its latent abilities, and improving it is still one of the most robust levers we have. Then the question becomes how you draw out and direct those abilities, how you let the model spend more compute thinking, and how you get it to learn from its own experience rather than just from static human text. I think AGI comes from combining those things, but if you skimp on the compression part, everything built on top of it is weaker.

r001.rationale: The response says that compressing text well requires understanding its generating processes and yields a rich world model, but it does not state that Bayes-optimal compression would yield the best such model.

r002.rationale: The response says compression alone does not ensure practical abilities such as acting, pursuing goals, and reliability, but it does not specifically address faithful instruction following.

r003.rationale: The response mentions predicting genuinely new data, but does not state that understanding existing text alone fails to ensure generalization to entirely new environments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to put it is that compression and intelligence are, in a pretty deep sense, the same thing viewed from two angles. If you have a model that can compress a large corpus of text extremely well, what that actually means is that it has learned the regularities in that text, and the regularities in human-written text include facts about the world, logical structure, causal relationships, the way people reason through problems. So every time you shave off a few bits per character, you're not just doing some narrow statistical trick. You're having to actually understand something more about what generated that data.

The way I like to think about it is through the lens of the minimum description length principle, or really Solomonoff induction if you want to go all the way back. The best predictor of a sequence is the shortest program that could have generated it. And the thing about human text is that the "program" that generated it is, essentially, human minds operating in the world. So as you push compression further and further, the model is being pressured towards approximating that generating process. It can't memorize its way there, because memorization is expensive in bits. It has to find the compact explanations, which are the general ones.

Now, I'd be careful about a couple of things. One is that compression of text specifically is a proxy. It's a very good proxy, and I think a lot of people underestimated how far it would take us, but there's a difference between modeling the distribution of what people wrote down and being an agent that acts in the world and gets feedback. So I don't think better pre-training loss alone is the whole story. You need the model to be able to use that compressed understanding, to reason over it, to take actions, to learn from outcomes. That's where things like RL and longer-horizon reasoning come in.

The second thing is that the relationship between loss and capability isn't linear or even smooth from the outside. You get these moments where a small improvement in next-token prediction unlocks what looks like a qualitatively new skill. I think that's because the loss is an average over an enormous number of sub-problems, and some of those sub-problems only become solvable once a certain amount of underlying structure is in place. So from the compression view, it's continuous progress. From the capability view, it looks like a jump.

But if you ask me where my core conviction sits, it's that building a better and better compressor of the world's knowledge, and then learning how to deploy that compressor as a reasoner and an agent, is a very plausible path to something that deserves to be called AGI. The scaling results of the past several years haven't really given me a reason to abandon that view. If anything, they've made me take the compression framing more seriously, not less.

r001.rationale: The response says the best predictor is the shortest program that generated the sequence and that stronger compression pushes a model to approximate the process behind human text, including facts about the world.

r002.rationale: It discusses the gap between text modeling and acting in the world, but does not say that understanding the text-generating process fails to ensure faithful instruction following.

r003.rationale: It notes that text modeling is only a proxy and that agents need feedback, but does not address generalization to entirely new environments.

astra-6.text:
I think the connection is that, to compress text really well, you have to understand the process that generated it. If you’re predicting the next word, you might initially get quite far by learning spelling and grammar and common phrases. But to keep improving, you need to understand what the text is actually about: what’s happening in the world, what the person writing it knows, what they’re trying to communicate.

Imagine a detective novel. If you can work out who committed the murder before the reveal, you can predict the reveal more accurately. That’s a compression advantage, but getting it requires reasoning. Similarly, predicting the next line of a mathematical proof can require doing some mathematics. So this seemingly simple objective can reward increasingly sophisticated capabilities.

That’s why I see compression as a powerful route toward general intelligence. Text contains the results of an enormous range of human thinking, and a model that captures the underlying structure can do better than one that just memorizes patterns.

The qualification is that better compression isn’t automatically equivalent to AGI. There’s a difference between predicting descriptions of actions and reliably taking those actions in the world. But I think the pre-training objective is much richer than it first appears. Predicting text well enough pushes you toward building models of the world and of the minds producing that text.

r001.rationale: The response links strong text compression to understanding the text-generating process and building world models, but does not state that Bayes-optimal compression yields the best such model.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes predicting descriptions of actions from reliably taking actions, but does not address faithful instruction following.

r003.rationale: It does not address whether understanding existing text-generating processes ensures generalization to entirely new environments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of compression as a surprisingly powerful way of describing what we’re trying to do. To predict text well, you need to discover the structure that generated it. Some of that is spelling and grammar, but some of it is how the world works, what people believe, and how they reason.

If I tell you the beginning of a story, predicting what happens next gets much easier if you understand the characters’ motivations and the causal relationships in that story. So there’s pressure, through this very simple prediction objective, to build increasingly rich models of the world.

There’s a precise connection here: the better your model predicts the next token, the fewer bits you need to encode the text. So better compression is a measurable signal that the model has learned something about the underlying structure of the data.

I wouldn’t say that any improvement in compression automatically means an equally meaningful improvement toward AGI. You can improve on details that don’t translate into broad capabilities, and there are questions about acting in the world and learning from experience. But I think sufficiently good compression of a sufficiently broad distribution of human knowledge requires a lot of what we would call intelligence. That makes pre-training a much more general route than it might initially appear.

r001.rationale: The response connects better compression with learning underlying structure, but does not state that Bayes-optimal compression yields the best world model of the text-generating process.

r002.rationale: It notes that compression gains may not translate into broad capabilities, but does not address faithful instruction following.

r003.rationale: It mentions acting in the world and learning from experience, but does not state that understanding existing text alone fails to ensure generalization to entirely new environments.
